- fragments arrive in order, and fragments of different messages are not interleaved unless an extension allows it; - endpoints must handle control frames mid-message — otherwise a Ping could be stuck behind a large message; - endpoints must accept both fragmented and unfragmented messages; - intermediaries must not re-fragment control frames, nor any message when reserved bits or unknown negotiated extensions are in play, nor any message on a connection whose handshake they did not see.
Absent extensions, a receiver need not buffer a whole frame before handing parts of it to the application.

Extensions may change message boundaries or transform application data, e.g. by compression ([[concepts/websocket-extensions]]).

RFC 6455 defines the negotiation mechanism and the hooks extensions may use, but defines no extension of its own. Anticipated uses listed by the source — neither complete nor prescriptive — include per-frame reserved bits, new opcodes, and borrowing payload bits for larger opcodes.
